<!-- =======================================================
     STORY
     ======================================================= -->

<section class="fff-section">

  <div class="fff-container fff-story-grid">

    <div class="fff-story-heading">

      <span class="fff-eyebrow">
        The Story
      </span>

      <h2>
        Bringing permaculture experience home to Florida
      </h2>

    </div>


    <div class="fff-story-copy">

      <p>
        Ryan was born and raised in Central Florida, but his approach to
        growing food was shaped far beyond his home state. He spent time
        living and working on permaculture farms in Hawaii and Costa
        Rica, including an off-grid farm where food, water, compost, and
        other daily resources were produced directly on the property.
      </p>

      <p>
        He eventually brought those experiences home and began adapting
        them to the conditions just north of Tampa. Today, Food Forest
        Florida is filled with tropical fruit trees, edible understory
        plants, compost systems, experimental seedlings, and growing
        methods designed around the property’s existing oak trees.
      </p>

      <p>
        The garden is not presented as a finished landscape. It is a
        place of continuous observation and experimentation. Ryan grows
        avocados and citrus from seed, tests cold protection strategies,
        grafts promising local fruit, and constantly looks for plants
        capable of thriving in his soil and climate.
      </p>

      <div class="fff-quote">
        The defining idea behind this garden is simple: work with the
        landscape, test what is possible, and allow successful plants to
        reveal what truly belongs there.
      </div>

    </div>

  </div>

</section>


<!-- =======================================================
     WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
     ======================================================= -->

<section class="fff-section fff-learn">

  <div class="fff-container">

    <div class="fff-section-header">

      <span class="fff-eyebrow">
        What You’ll Learn
      </span>

      <h2>
        Practical ideas from the tour
      </h2>

      <p>
        Ryan explains the reasoning behind nearly every part of the
        food forest, from tree placement and composting to genetics and
        cold protection.
      </p>

    </div>


    <div class="fff-learn-grid">

      <article class="fff-learn-card">

        <span class="fff-learn-number">1</span>

        <h3>Use existing trees to create microclimates</h3>

        <p>
          Oak canopies provide dappled shade and protection from cold,
          wind, and storms while creating planting opportunities for
          citrus, pineapples, and other sensitive crops.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-learn-card">

        <span class="fff-learn-number">2</span>

        <h3>Build garden beds from local materials</h3>

        <p>
          Fallen and dying trees become log borders that hold compost,
          wood chips, fungi, and organic matter while gradually helping
          create new soil.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-learn-card">

        <span class="fff-learn-number">3</span>

        <h3>Grow seedlings as long-term experiments</h3>

        <p>
          Seed-grown citrus and avocados may reveal useful genetics,
          stronger local adaptation, or dependable root systems that
          can later support grafted varieties.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-learn-card">

        <span class="fff-learn-number">4</span>

        <h3>Use plants to protect other plants</h3>

        <p>
          Ryan experiments with allowing established tropical foliage
          to surround sensitive jackfruit trees before winter, creating
          an additional layer of cold protection.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-learn-card">

        <span class="fff-learn-number">5</span>

        <h3>Turn waste into food forest fertility</h3>

        <p>
          Food scraps, leaves, coffee grounds, yard debris, and pruned
          plant material are continually returned to the system through
          composting and banana circles.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-learn-card">

        <span class="fff-learn-number">6</span>

        <h3>Choose varieties for local conditions</h3>

        <p>
          Wind tolerance, cold tolerance, productivity, mature size,
          and resistance to local pests can matter as much as flavor
          when choosing fruit varieties for Central Florida.
        </p>

      </article>

    </div>

  </div>

</section>

     ======================================================= -->

<section class="fff-section fff-secret">

    </div>


    <div>

      <span class="fff-eyebrow">
        The Secret Garden
      </span>

      <h2>
        A productive garden hidden among the oak trees
      </h2>

      <p>
        Ryan calls this section his secret garden because it is tucked
        beneath the property’s mature oak canopy. Rather than removing
        those trees, he uses their shade, leaf litter, roots, and
        protection as part of the growing system.
      </p>

      <p>
        Old logs form the edges of the garden beds. Unfinished compost
        and wood chips fill the spaces between them. Over time, fungi
        and decomposers help transform those materials into fertile
        growing areas.
      </p>

      <div class="fff-secret-points">

        <div class="fff-secret-point">
          Fallen logs become garden-bed borders and fungal habitat.
        </div>

        <div class="fff-secret-point">
          Oak canopy creates shade and protection from extreme weather.
        </div>

        <div class="fff-secret-point">
          Compost and wood chips gradually build new soil.
        </div>

        <div class="fff-secret-point">
          Edible plants occupy multiple layers beneath the canopy.
        </div>

      </div>

    </div>

  </div>

</section>


<!-- =======================================================
     PHILOSOPHY
     ======================================================= -->

<section class="fff-section">

  <div class="fff-container">

    <div class="fff-section-header">

      <span class="fff-eyebrow">
        Ryan’s Growing Philosophy
      </span>

      <h2>
        A food forest built through observation
      </h2>

      <p>
        Rather than relying on a rigid plan, Ryan continually studies
        how plants respond and adjusts the garden around what succeeds.
      </p>

    </div>


    <div class="fff-philosophy-grid">

      <article class="fff-philosophy-card">

        <span class="fff-philosophy-icon" aria-hidden="true">🌱</span>

        <h3>Experiment with seedlings</h3>

        <p>
          Seeds create the possibility of trees better adapted to local
          soil, weather, pests, and cold.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-philosophy-card">

        <span class="fff-philosophy-icon" aria-hidden="true">🌳</span>

        <h3>Work with the canopy</h3>

        <p>
          Existing oak trees are treated as valuable infrastructure,
          not obstacles that need to be removed.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-philosophy-card">

        <span class="fff-philosophy-icon" aria-hidden="true">♻️</span>

        <h3>Return organic matter</h3>

        <p>
          Food scraps, coffee grounds, leaves, logs, and yard debris are
          transformed into fertility.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-philosophy-card">

        <span class="fff-philosophy-icon" aria-hidden="true">🧪</span>

        <h3>Keep testing ideas</h3>

        <p>
          Cold protection, grafting, air layering, variety selection,
          and plant combinations remain ongoing experiments.
        </p>

      </article>

    </div>

  </div>

</section>

<!-- =======================================================
     GROWING SYSTEMS
     ======================================================= -->

<section class="fff-section">

  <div class="fff-container">

    <div class="fff-section-header">

      <span class="fff-eyebrow">
        Growing Systems
      </span>

      <h2>
        How fertility and protection move through the property
      </h2>

    </div>


    <div class="fff-systems-grid">

      <article class="fff-system-card">

        <h3>Three-Bin Compost System</h3>

        <p>
          Food scraps and coffee grounds begin in the freshest bin,
          then move through the system until they become finished
          compost for the fruit trees.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-system-card">

        <h3>Banana Circle</h3>

        <p>
          Yard waste is placed in the center of a ring of bananas,
          where it breaks down and releases nutrients for the
          surrounding plants.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-system-card">

        <h3>Oak Microclimates</h3>

        <p>
          Citrus, pineapples, and other crops are placed beneath mature
          oak trees to benefit from shade, leaf litter, and protection
          from wind and cold.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-system-card">

        <h3>Living Cold Protection</h3>

        <p>
          Large tropical foliage is allowed to grow around sensitive
          fruit trees, potentially creating a warmer and more protected
          pocket during winter.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-system-card">

        <h3>Air Layering and Grafting</h3>

        <p>
          Successful plants are propagated, promising local fruit is
          grafted, and seedlings remain available as rootstock or
          future varieties.
        </p>

      </article>


      <article class="fff-system-card">

        <h3>Layered Polycultures</h3>

        <p>
          Bananas, moringa, mulberries, sugar cane, guava, ice cream
          bean, sugar apple, and other species share growing areas
          instead of being separated into isolated rows.
        </p>

      </article>

    </div>

  </div>

</section>

<!-- =======================================================
     TAKEAWAY
     ======================================================= -->

<section class="fff-section">

  <div class="fff-container">

    <div class="fff-takeaway-card">

      <span class="fff-eyebrow">
        The Takeaway
      </span>

      <h2>
        A resilient food forest grows through curiosity
      </h2>

      <p>
        Food Forest Florida demonstrates that a productive landscape
        does not need to begin with perfect soil, a completely open
        property, or a finished master plan. Ryan works with the oak
        trees already present, returns waste materials to the soil,
        observes which seedlings survive, and treats every challenge as
        an opportunity to learn. The result is a food forest that
        continues to evolve with every season.
      </p>

    </div>

  </div>

</section>
